soil-bio-283.title: Sporosarcina pasteurii, the bacterium that turns sand to stone
soil-bio-283.text: Give one soil bacterium calcium and urea, and loose sand sets solid. Sporosarcina pasteurii is a gram-positive, rod-shaped bacterium, 0.5 to 1.2 micrometres wide and 1.3 to 4.0 micrometres long. It forms endospores and thrives at pH 9 to 10, surviving up to pH 11.2. It secretes urease to hydrolyse urea, which feeds it nitrogen, carbon and energy. The carbonate ions released react with calcium to precipitate {{ref:soil-found-118}} that cements sand grains. This is {{ref:soil-bio-067}}. The organism is non-pathogenic and makes a great deal of urease, so it is a common choice for the job. It is proposed for self-healing concrete and other bio-cement uses.

soil-bio-221.title: Metagenomics: reading the DNA of a whole soil
soil-bio-221.text:
A single gram of soil holds about 10^9 to 10^10 microbial cells, and roughly one gigabase of sequence. Metagenomics studies all the genetic material from every organism in such a sample, revealing composition, diversity and functional potential. It profiles communities without culturing species, and early environmental gene studies showed that cultivation had missed most microbial diversity. Norman Pace proposed cloning DNA directly from environmental samples in 1985, and his group first reported doing so in 1991.

It differs from amplicon sequencing, or metabarcoding. That method reads marker genes and shows which taxa are present. The 16S rRNA gene identifies bacteria and archaea, and 18S rRNA or ITS identifies fungi; more similar sequences are taken to mean closer evolutionary relatedness. Metagenomics sequences all the DNA, so it also recovers enzymes and pathways. Functional metagenomics explores plant-microbe interactions and the roles of uncultivated or rare members in nutrient cycling and plant growth.

There is a catch. Sampling is uncontrolled, so the most abundant organisms dominate shotgun sequence data. Long-read sequencing of soils in industrial zones showed that chronic heavy metal contamination restructures the soil microbial community. Soil communities are among the most complex known, which makes {{ref:soil-bio-011}}, {{ref:soil-bio-008}} and the {{ref:soil-bio-227}} natural targets.

soil-bio-273.title: Fungal biocontrol: fungi that fight crop disease
soil-bio-273.text: About 300 species of fungi and fungus-like organisms, in 13 classes and 113 genera, are used as biocontrol agents against plant fungal diseases. They protect crops in two ways. Some parasitise other fungi, and organisms that do so are called mycoparasitic. Others compete with pathogenic bacteria or fungi for nutrients and space, by the competitive exclusion principle. Both tactics rely on the habits of the {{ref:soil-bio-271}} itself.

soil-bio-272.title: How fungi reproduce and spread
soil-bio-272.text: Fungi reproduce asexually, sexually or both, and spread mainly by spores. Asexual reproduction uses vegetative spores, called conidia, or mycelial fragmentation, in which pieces of mycelium each grow into a separate mycelium. An estimated third of fungi use more than one method, with a sexual teleomorph stage and an asexual anamorph stage. Spores of most studied species travel by wind. Dry, hydrophobic spores are readily scattered by raindrops. Everything here builds on the basic body of the {{ref:soil-bio-271}}.

soil-bio-276.title: Humus: the dark, stable core of soil organic matter
soil-bio-276.text:
Humus is light for its bulk. Its bulk density is just 0.05 to 0.25 g per cubic centimetre, and its cation exchange capacity tops 200 cmol(+) per kilogram. It is the stable, dark, amorphous fraction of soil organic matter left after most added residues have decomposed, bound to clays and oxides that shield it from microbes. It has high porosity and water holding capacity. Its approximate composition is 50% carbon, 35% oxygen, 8% hydrogen, 5% nitrogen and 2% sulfur.

It commonly supplies 20 to 30% or more of a soil's cation exchange capacity, buffers pH and binds peds into aggregates. Arable soils average 2 to 3% humus, from under 1% to over 12%.

Keeping it takes work. Cultivated soils lose humus by decomposition at 1 to 2% per year. Holding the normal level needs 1000 to 5000 kg per hectare of organic material a year, since added material does not permanently raise it. Rotations with grasses and legumes, conservation tillage and residue management help sustain it.

soil-bio-275.title: From residue to humus: how microbes recycle organic matter
soil-bio-275.text:
Soil with 1% organic matter holds up to 45 million kilocalories per acre-furrow-slice, equivalent to about 6 tons of coal. Microbes oxidise that energy store partly to carbon dioxide, water and energy, leaving humus, new microbial cells and inorganic plant nutrients.

Fresh residues decompose rapidly at first, releasing carbon dioxide, water, energy and small amounts of inorganic nitrogen, phosphorus and sulfur. The microbes' most important function is recycling organic carbon to CO2, which keeps photosynthesis going. Their oxidation also turns nutrients from unavailable organic forms into plant-available inorganic ones, so organic matter acts as a slow-release fertilizer that buffers nutrient supply.

The process is wasteful. Microbes use only a small share of the energy for new cells, and making one pound of soil organic matter may destroy 10 to 20 pounds of residues. Fresh residues also accelerate decomposition of humified material already in the soil. The reward is structure. Added organic matter improves tilth, raises cation exchange and water holding capacity and aeration, and reduces erosion.

soil-bio-277.title: What controls the number of microbes in soil
soil-bio-277.text: Soil organisms make up under 0.5% of dry soil mass. Their numbers depend on temperature, moisture, pH, nutrients, energy supply and oxygen. Decay organisms work best at about 20 to 40 degrees C, and most others slow outside that range. Too much water cuts numbers and kinds through poor aeration, yet at low moisture soil organisms do better than higher plants. Below pH 6.0 fungi become the dominant microorganisms. Adding organisms to a soil is usually ineffective because the community, described in {{ref:soil-bio-011}}, is already vast. Changing the crop alters populations more.

soil-bio-281.title: How healthy soil holds pests in check
soil-bio-281.text: In any given year only a small number of bacteria, fungi, insects and nematodes might harm plants, and a diverse soil reduces their impact. Diverse soil organisms keep checks and balances that stop disease organisms and parasites from becoming major problems, a payoff of {{ref:soil-bio-008}}. Some fungi kill nematodes or insects, and some produce antibiotics. Protozoa, springtails and mites eat disease-causing fungi and bacteria. Trichoderma and Pseudomonas fluorescens colonize roots and protect them, and Bacillus thuringiensis toxin is sold as a biological control agent. Suppression is thought to arise from competition for nutrients, antagonistic substances or direct parasitism. Some beneficial organisms also induce plant immune defenses.

soil-bio-280.title: Roots as soil engineers
soil-bio-280.text: Corn sends about 20 percent of its photosynthesis sugars to its roots early to mid-season. Roots influence soil as much as soil influences them, shaping aggregates and feeding soil organisms. Root pressure brings particles closer, small roots bind them, and root hairs add soil contact for water and nutrient access and help form aggregates. Roots exude compounds that feed organisms in the surrounding zone. Mucigel, a sticky layer around roots, gives close contact between microorganisms, soil minerals and the plant. Roots add organic matter that may decompose more slowly than surface residues, and in grasses the living tissue below ground can exceed that above. They do not grow well in compact, nutrient- or water-poor, high-pathogen or extreme-pH soil.

soil-hist-015.title: The Winogradsky column: a jar of sediment as an ecosystem
soil-hist-015.text: A jar of mud can teach a whole course in microbial metabolism. A Winogradsky column is a simple stratified microbial ecosystem built from sediment in a container. Columns are set up as a control and with added carbon (cellulose), sulfur (egg yolk calcium sulfate) or both, then form oxygen and sulfide gradients, the kind described in {{ref:soil-chem-121}}. Purple and green sulfur bacteria use sulfide to support photosynthesis, and green sulfur bacteria tolerate higher sulfide than purple. Winogradsky developed it, and discovered chemosynthesis, in his early efforts to understand microbes outside the medical context. It remains an important demonstration of chemoautotrophy and microbial ecology in microbiology lectures around the world, and a window into {{ref:soil-bio-011}}.

soil-bio-278.title: Free-living bacteria that fix nitrogen
soil-bio-278.text: Plants and animals cannot use nitrogen gas, or nitrogen locked in organic molecules. It must be converted to ammonium and nitrate, a bacterial process called nitrogen mineralization. Some free-living soil bacteria take nitrogen gas from the air and turn it into a form plants can use to make amino acids and proteins. Azospirillum and Azotobacter are free-living fixers, and Azospirillum attaches to root surfaces and makes substances that help plants tolerate stress. They add only modest nitrogen, but it matters in natural systems where nutrient cycling is efficient. Rhizobia in legume root nodules do far more, receiving sugars from the plant and supplying usable nitrogen. An alfalfa stand may fix hundreds of pounds per acre a year, peas about 30 to 50. All of these are {{ref:soil-bio-002}} working alongside {{ref:soil-bio-003}}.

soil-bio-282.title: Soil organisms span ten orders of magnitude
soil-bio-282.text:
The smallest soil bacterium is about 0.5 micrometres across. Some forest fungi form mycelia of 1 km or more. Soil organisms span nearly ten orders of magnitude in size. Soil-dwelling amphibians and mammals are about 10 cm long, and roots run 0.1 to 10 m. A colony of Armillaria ostoyae in an Oregon Douglas fir forest covers several square kilometres and may be the largest organism by area.

Traditional groups are microflora, macroflora (roots), microfauna, mesofauna (0.1 to 2 mm metazoans) and macrofauna (over 2 mm). The scheme confuses, since fungi are called microflora yet are macroscopic and heterotrophic. Even the basic map changed late. Archaea were widely recognized as distinct from bacteria only in the early 1990s. DNA analysis shows them as different from bacteria as from plants or animals, in Woese's three domains Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya. The cast spans {{ref:soil-bio-001}}, {{ref:soil-bio-002}}, {{ref:soil-bio-003}}, {{ref:soil-bio-012}}, {{ref:soil-bio-016}} and {{ref:soil-bio-023}}, and gives a measure of {{ref:soil-bio-008}}.

soil-bio-279.title: Soil insects and arthropods
soil-bio-279.text: Soil insects such as termites, springtails, ants, fly larvae and beetles are often secondary and tertiary consumers in the {{ref:soil-bio-025}}. Springtails eat fungi and animal remains and are prey for predacious mites. Many beetles eat other soil animals, and dung beetles bury manure balls. Millipedes are primary consumers of plant residues, while centipedes eat other organisms. Mites eat fungi, other mites, insect eggs or residues, and spiders hold insect pests down. Termites eat wood and also decomposed organic residues in soil.

soil-bio-322.title: Klebsiella oxytoca, a nitrogen fixer on barley roots
soil-bio-322.text: Klebsiella oxytoca is a Gram-negative, rod-shaped bacterium, closely related to K. pneumoniae and distinguished from it by indole production. It is a diazotroph: it colonises plant hosts and fixes atmospheric nitrogen into a form the plant can use. It has been shown to associate with the barley {{ref:soil-bio-143}} through an entire vegetative period. The bacteria adhere strongly to root hairs and less strongly to the elongation zone and root cap mucilage.

soil-bio-321.title: Epiphytes: plants that live on plants
soil-bio-321.text: Orchids never touch the ground, yet they live well. An epiphyte is a plant or plant-like organism that grows on the surface of another plant, taking moisture and nutrients from air, rain or accumulated debris. It uses the host, called the phorophyte, only for support and, unlike parasitic plants, draws no nourishment from it. It is not rooted in soil. Without soil it depends on fog, dew, rain, mist, nutrients leached or decomposed from rooted plants, and nitrogen fixation. Holo-epiphytes never touch the ground, like orchids; hemi-epiphytes such as strangler figs spend only part of life off the ground. Epiphytes hold water in the canopy, reducing water input to the soil, and cool and moisten the host canopy, which may cut its transpiration.

soil-found-045.title: Soil organic matter: the small fraction that shapes everything
soil-found-045.text:
Soil organic matter is present in small amounts, typically 1 to 6% by weight in agricultural soil, yet it strongly affects almost all soil properties. It is about twice the organic carbon level. Its parts are described as the living, the dead and the very dead. They are living organisms, fresh residues, and molecules from well-decomposed residues.

The living part is about 15% of soil organic matter, and soil organisms are estimated at about 25% of the world's biodiversity. Fresh residues, the active fraction, feed soil organisms and release nutrients. Easily decomposed molecules like proteins, amino acids, sugars and starches do not last long, while lignin decomposes more slowly. Waterlogged peats and mucks hold much undecomposed organic matter that does not give the benefits of fresh residues.

Organic matter also builds structure. Sticky substances on earthworm skin and fungal products bind particles, and sticky root substances plus fine roots and mycorrhizae promote stable aggregates. Organic compounds produced as fresh residues decompose also bind soil particles and give good structure. Earthworms and some fungi make channels that improve infiltration, water status and aeration. The link to {{ref:soil-bio-001}} is direct, since the living part is the soil's biology.

soil-found-050.title: How climate decides how much organic matter a soil holds
soil-found-050.text:
Cold soils are rich in organic matter and hot ones are poor. Temperature, soil moisture and topography are the main factors in how much accumulates. In the US, warmer southern climates hold less: more vegetation grows, but faster decomposition by more active organisms for longer each year becomes the dominant influence. Heavy rain and heat in the tropics speed decomposition and nutrient leaching, so forests there depend on efficient recycling of nutrients by living biomass.

Organic matter builds up where cold or waterlogging, which makes soil anaerobic, slows decomposers. Arctic and alpine soils receive little in their short growing seasons but are rich in it because cold slows decomposition. Warming and thawing now release it as CO2 and methane. Arid soils usually have little, because plant growth and decomposition are low, though rain triggers a rapid burst of decomposition. Generally it rises with annual precipitation as more plant growth returns more residue, though wet, poorly aerated soils decompose it more slowly. Steep slopes under cultivation encourage erosion of the topsoil, which holds most of the raw material that would otherwise become humus. See {{ref:soil-found-045}}.

soil-found-049.title: Soil organic matter in the global carbon cycle
soil-found-049.text:
The largest amount of carbon on land is stored in soil organic matter, not in living plants. It holds about four times as much as plants, and world soils hold two to three times the atmosphere's amount. Seven inches of soil with 1% organic matter holds as much carbon as the air above a field. The global soil carbon pool is estimated at 2,500 gigatons, 3.3 times the atmospheric pool of 750 gigatons and 4.5 times the biotic pool of 560 gigatons. Organic carbon, mostly as {{ref:soil-found-045}}, accounts for about 1,550 gigatons. The rest is soil inorganic carbon, mainly carbonates and bicarbonates.

Plants remove carbon dioxide from the air using sunlight and build organic molecules. Plants and animals release it again by respiration, and burning fuels adds more. As organic matter is depleted the soil becomes a carbon dioxide source. Clearing and burning forest, then rapid loss under agriculture, gives a secondary, often larger flush. Agricultural conversion of forests and grasslands is second only to fossil fuel burning as a contributor to rising atmospheric CO2.

Soils managed to build organic matter can become net carbon sinks. It is no silver bullet, but on a massive scale it can slow CO2 increase for a while and also raises soil resilience to storms and dry spells.

soil-bio-284.title: Polysaccharides: sugar chains that store and build
soil-bio-284.text:
Wood, paper and cotton are all sugar chains. Polysaccharides are large polymers of monosaccharides linked by glycosidic bonds, ranging from linear to highly branched. Storage types include starch, glycogen and galactogen. Structural ones include cellulose, hemicellulose, chitin and pectin. Plant structural parts are mostly cellulose; wood is largely cellulose and lignin, while paper and cotton are nearly pure cellulose.

Many organisms digest starch to glucose, but few can metabolize cellulose. Some bacteria and protists can, and ruminants and termites use microorganisms to process it. Humans and many animals lack an enzyme for the beta-linkages, so cellulose is indigestible except where gut bacteria supply it. Chitin yields to chitinase enzymes secreted by bacteria, fungi and some plants. Microbes that detect chitin make enzymes that cleave it to simple sugars and ammonia. It is closely related to chitosan, a more water-soluble derivative. Bacteria, fungi and algae often secrete polysaccharides to adhere to surfaces and avoid drying out, and polysaccharide matrices enclose bacterial biofilms. See {{ref:soil-bio-115}} and the {{ref:soil-bio-271}}.

soil-bio-285.title: How organic matter feeds plants
soil-bio-285.text:
Plants need 17 elements. Carbon and oxygen come from air and the rest mainly from soil, with availability affected directly or indirectly by organic matter, the heart of soil fertility. Decomposition converts nutrients to plant-usable forms, produces cation exchange capacity that retains calcium, potassium, magnesium and ammonium, and makes organic molecules that hold micronutrients such as zinc and iron. Siderophores make micronutrients more available, so roots grow longer and more branched. Humic substances may stimulate roots by raising micronutrient availability and changing gene expression. In one experiment humic acids in nutrient solution increased tomato and corn growth and root branching. Soil organisms fix nitrogen and dissolve phosphorus, and with too little food they are scarce and more fertilizer is needed.

Physical effects matter as well. Organic matter improves structure, raising infiltration, water-holding capacity and root growth into permeable soil. Good tilth stores more water between rains and reduces erosion. Poor tilth means broken aggregates, compaction, and less aeration and water storage, and a layer can become too compact for roots. Topsoil's good qualities arise because it is rich in organic matter and life, not because of its position. See {{ref:soil-found-045}}, {{ref:soil-bio-089}} and {{ref:soil-found-014}}.
